newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Phillips sees limited Sumitomo effect.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Phillips sees limited Sumitomo effect.

text.p: Although Sumitomo Corp's $1.8 billion losses in copper trading shocked world markets, the crisis has not cascaded to other market participants, Fed Governor Susan Phillips said.
Sumitomo is meeting all of its obligations on copper transactions with U.S. banks, Phillips said in prepared testimony for a House Banking Committee hearing.

"At this time, the losses appear to be limited to the Sumitomo trading company, which has been meeting all of its obligations to U.S. banks arising from its transactions in the copper market," Phillips said.
The copper market has stabilized and the Fed is not aware of any "material spill-over effects to other markets," Phillips added.
Phillips said the crisis did not indicate a need for more regulation but perhaps for greater disclosure of risk levels by market participants.
"Losses such as Sumitomo's raise the issue of more extensive regulation," Phillips said. "Regulation, however, simply cannot substitute for sound management."
"A more appropriate response, indeed for non-financial companies the only practical response, is to continue to promote policies that foster greater market discipline," Phillips said.
Encouraging greater disclosure of risks would "move in that direction," she added.
Phillips noted that commodity derivatives activity at U.S. banks remains limited.
J.P. Morgan & Co and Chase Manhattan Corp loaned Sumitomo hundreds of millions of dollars through derivative contracts tied to the copper markets, sources familiar with the transactions have said.

"Commodities trading at U.S. banks remains a very small component of their overall activities," Phillips said. "Even their trading of physical commodities contracts on organized exchanges through privately negotiated transactions is small, accounting for less than one percent of all their derivatives positions."
